guideTitle: Best Monochrome Laser Printers for Home Offices (2026)
metaTitle: Best Monochrome Laser Printers for Home Offices
metaDescription: Six monochrome laser printers for home offices compared on duplex, feeders, speed and scanning, with picks for solo workers, shared desks and busy small teams.
expertTake: The Brother DCP-L2640DW is the best overall home office mono laser because it combines duplex, scanning and a fast engine at a sensible price tier. The Brother HL-L2460DW is the value pick for print-only desks. Anyone who regularly prints color presentations or photos should skip monochrome lasers entirely.
introParagraphs: For a home office that lives on contracts, invoices, reports and shipping paperwork, a black and white laser is the most economical tool. The toner is a dry powder, so the machine sits idle through a slow month without clogging, and the pages come out dry and ready to sign.

The choice splits along a few lines: whether you want a scanner and feeder or just a printer, whether duplex is automatic, how fast the engine runs and how the machine joins your network. The sections below sort those decisions by the way an office actually works day to day.

products.name: Brother DCP-L2640DW Mono Laser All-in-One, 36 ppm
products.description:
Brother engineered this multifunction as the default choice for a one or two person office. The 36 page per minute engine is the fastest in the lineup alongside its fax-equipped sibling, and automatic two-sided printing is included, so a forty page report does not tie up the evening.

Its compromise is that it leaves out fax, which the Brother MFC-L2820DW adds for a similar price tier. It also lacks the 50-sheet auto document feeder that the HP LaserJet Pro 3101sdw advertises, so heavy scanning will feel slower here. For an office that scans a handful of pages and prints a lot, those omissions are easy to live with.

In ownership terms the Brother laser design is plain: one drum and toner path, few moving parts and driver software that behaves on Windows and Mac. Standard and high-yield toner sizes are sold, and the high-yield cartridge is what keeps cost per page low in an office that prints daily. Keep the scanner glass wiped and the paper stored flat, and it should stay dependable through years of steady use.
products.bestFor: Solo professionals who print long documents and scan a few pages a day.

products.name: Brother MFC-L2820DW Mono Laser All-in-One with Fax
products.description:
The MFC-L2820DW is the DCP-L2640DW with a fax modem added, aimed at small offices that still receive faxed forms from clinics, lenders or government. It keeps the 36 page per minute rate and dual-band wireless on 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz, and the listing calls out secure connection to multiple devices.

The tradeoff is paying for a fax function that many offices have abandoned. If you do not send or receive faxes, the DCP-L2640DW delivers the same speed and the same print quality for less. Choose this model only if a real workflow demands fax, such as a legal or medical practice working from home.

Ownership matches its sibling, with Brother toner in standard and high-yield sizes. The fax board needs a landline or an analog adapter, which is an extra cost and setup step that buyers sometimes forget. Treat the telephone connection as a one-time install and the machine runs like any other Brother laser.

products.name: HP LaserJet MFP M235sdw Duplex Mono Laser, 28 ppm
products.description:
HP built the M235sdw around speed in two-sided jobs, advertising the fastest duplex printing in its class and a Wi-Fi radio that detects and repairs connection problems on its own. The up to 28 page per minute single-sided rate is lower than Brother's 36, but the duplex pass is where it claims the lead.

The weak spot is raw single-sided speed and Brother's mature drivers. If your jobs are mostly one-sided, the Brother DCP-L2640DW is faster; if they are two-sided packets, the HP narrows the gap. Self-resetting Wi-Fi is a real benefit for an office where the router is far away or the network drops overnight.

Ownership centers on HP toner and firmware policy. Genuine HP cartridges are the safe route, and firmware changes can alter how third-party toner is treated, so read the terms before you buy a replacement. Keep the scanner glass clean and the unit behaves like a quiet workhorse.
products.bestFor: Offices that print many two-sided packets over Wi-Fi.

cons: Single-sided speed trails the Brother 36 ppm

products.name: HP LaserJet Pro 3101sdw Mono Laser All-in-One, 250-Sheet Tray
products.description:
The 3101sdw is the paper-handling specialist of this roundup. A 250-sheet input tray holds a full short ream, and a 50-sheet automatic document feeder lets you scan or copy a stack unattended, which no other model here matches.

The tradeoff is bulk and tier. It is larger than the HP LaserJet MFP M235sdw and sits higher in the price ladder, so it is overkill for a desk that prints ten pages a day. If your work involves copying contracts, scanning case files or feeding forms by the dozen, the feeder pays for itself quickly in time.

Ownership is about managing paper and toner. A bigger tray means fewer top-ups but more paper that can curl in humid rooms, so store reams sealed. HP sells standard and high-yield toner, and the larger cartridge makes sense for the volume this machine invites. Dust the feeder rollers every few months to keep multi-page scans straight.

products.name: Brother HL-L2460DW Dual-Band Duplex Mono Laser
products.description:
When an office only needs documents out, the HL-L2460DW delivers that with the fewest moving parts. It pairs automatic duplex with dual-band wireless and an Ethernet port, and Brother's mobile app lets you manage the machine from a phone.

What you give up is the absence of any scanner. If someone in the house needs to scan, that job falls to a phone app or a separate device, which is why the Brother DCP-L2640DW exists a rung above. The Ethernet port matters for a home office with a wired desk, since a cable removes the router from the printing path.

Ownership is easy: toner is the sole running cost, the paper path is short and the print-only body has no scanner glass to scratch. Starter toner is a partial fill, so budget for a replacement cartridge early. A machine like this is happiest on a shelf near the router.
products.bestFor: Print-only desks that want duplex and a wired option.

Automatic duplex included

cons: Speed is lower than the 36 ppm multifunctions

products.name: HP LaserJet M209d Wired Duplex Mono Laser
products.description:
The M209d is built for a single desk and a single computer. HP lists automatic two-sided printing, a 150-sheet input tray and a USB cable in the box, and it leaves wireless out of the pitch.

What you give up against the Brother HL-L2460DW is network reach: this is a one-computer printer unless you plug it into a router that offers a USB print server. What you gain is a duplex laser that never loses its connection, which suits an office with a desktop that stays powered.

There is little to maintain beyond toner and paper. Since the tray holds 150 sheets, long runs need a refill, and the compact shape fits under a monitor stand. Keep the USB cable seated and update the driver after a major operating system upgrade.
products.bestFor: Single-computer offices that want duplex through a plain cable.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A multifunction adds a flatbed, sometimes a feeder, and a screen, so it costs more and needs more cleaning. The Brother DCP-L2640DW and HP LaserJet MFP M235sdw scan and copy, while the Brother HL-L2460DW and HP M209d print only. Count how many pages you scan monthly before paying for the extra hardware.

A feeder lets you scan or copy a stack unattended, and its capacity sets how big a stack you can leave. The HP LaserJet Pro 3101sdw lists a 50-sheet feeder, which is a real time saver for contracts or tax paperwork. A flatbed alone means scanning one page at a time, which is tiring above a dozen sheets.

The Brother DCP-L2640DW and MFC-L2820DW reach up to 36 pages per minute, the HP M235sdw reaches up to 28. Speed only helps on documents over ten pages, because warm-up and first-page time dominate short jobs. Match the rating to your longest regular job.

Printers that drop off Wi-Fi create the most support calls. Dual-band wireless, as on the Brother HL-L2460DW and HP M235sdw, gives a second band to fall back on, and Ethernet takes the router radio out of the equation. The wired-only HP M209d never has this issue.

Fax is still a requirement for some medical, legal and financial work. The Brother MFC-L2820DW is the fax model in this lineup, but it requires a phone line or analog adapter. Pay for fax only when a real client asks for it.

A mono laser has no ink to dry, so the running cost is toner divided by its rated yield, quoted at five percent coverage. The high-yield cartridge is the sensible buy for an office printing daily. Check whether the starter toner in the box is a partial fill before you assume it will last.

specDecoder.meaning: Pages per minute is the sustained speed on plain text once the job is running. A higher rating shortens long reports.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Brother DCP-L2640DW lists up to 36 ppm while the HP M235sdw lists up to 28 ppm.

specDecoder.meaning: An ADF pulls sheets through the scanner without you touching them. Capacity is the number of sheets it holds.
Dual-band means the printer can join either the 2.4 GHz band or the 5 GHz band. The 5 GHz band is faster but shorter range.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Brother MFC-L2820DW and HL-L2460DW list dual-band, while the HP M209d is USB only.

specDecoder.meaning: Tray capacity is the number of sheets loaded at once. Larger trays reduce refills.
specDecoder.watchFor: The HP M209d holds 150 sheets and the HP 3101sdw holds 250.

specDecoder.meaning: Yield is the pages a cartridge can print at standard coverage. Dense pages use toner faster.
specDecoder.watchFor: Compare standard and high-yield cartridges for the Brother models before buying.

howWeEvaluated.title: Throughput
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared rated speeds across the lineup, from 28 pages per minute on the HP M235sdw to 36 on the Brother models. First-page time and duplex speed were considered alongside the headline rating. Long reports and short letters were treated as different jobs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Paper and scan handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked tray size, duplex and feeder capacity, with the HP 3101sdw's 50-sheet feeder as the benchmark. Models without a feeder lost points for stack scanning. Simple paper paths scored higher for jam resistance.

howWeEvaluated.title: Network behavior
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed dual-band Wi-Fi, Ethernet and USB, noting that the HP M209d is wired only. The HP M235sdw's self-reset feature earned credit for reliability. Mobile app support was part of ease of setup.

howWeEvaluated.title: Office fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched each machine to a work style, from the print-only Brother HL-L2460DW to the fax-capable Brother MFC-L2820DW. Features that most offices never use were noted rather than rewarded. Body size mattered for small desks.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership cost
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered toner yield choices, firmware policy on third-party cartridges and warranty terms. A mono laser gets credit for toner that survives idle months. Wear parts such as pickup rollers were counted as upkeep.

cards.label: Brother
cards.text: Brother's DCP-L2640DW, MFC-L2820DW and HL-L2460DW are known for straightforward drivers and a 36 page per minute engine on the multifunctions. Their strength is value and a simple paper path.

cards.label: HP
cards.text: HP's M235sdw and 3101sdw lean on feeder capacity, fast duplex and self-repairing Wi-Fi. Their trade is a stricter toner policy and a higher tier for the larger machines.

howToChoose.note: Pick Brother for value and speed; pick HP when a big feeder or fast duplex matters.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for automatic duplex, a feeder and a tray that matches your stack size. A fast engine matters less than paper handling when the work is copying and scanning contracts.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The HP LaserJet Pro 3101sdw is the strongest here for stack work with its 50-sheet feeder and 250-sheet tray. The Brother DCP-L2640DW is the pick if volume is mostly printing.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you scan stacks, where the HP 3101sdw saves minutes daily, or if you need fax, where the Brother MFC-L2820DW is the only option.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you print only, where the Brother HL-L2460DW or HP M209d covers duplex without a scanner you will not use.

faq.q: Is a monochrome laser enough for a home office?
faq.a: For text documents, forms and invoices, yes. It prints sharp black pages cheaply and does not dry out. If you need color charts, brochures or photos, you will want a color laser or an ink tank instead.

faq.q: Do I need a scanner in a home office laser?
faq.a: Only if you scan regularly. A flatbed handles single pages, and a feeder like the one on the HP 3101sdw handles stacks. A phone scanning app covers occasional receipts.

faq.q: How long do mono lasers last?
faq.a: Their simple design usually outlasts inkjets, and toner survives idle months. The wear items are rollers and the fuser, so keep paper clean and the vents clear.

faq.q: Is 36 pages per minute really that much faster than 28?
faq.a: On a long document it saves a minute or two. On short jobs the first-page time and warm-up matter more, so the gap is hard to notice.
Most offices do not, but some medical, legal and government workflows still use it. If a client requires it, the Brother MFC-L2820DW is the fax model here.

faq.q: Can I save money with third-party toner?
faq.a: Sometimes, but firmware updates can block non-original cartridges, and some warranties assume genuine toner. Read the policy for your model first.
